strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically relevant gap: SAM3's noun-phrase-only concept prompting cannot handle rich, multi-condition natural-language instructions, and the paper's taxonomy (concept/simple/complex) is a clean and sensible framing of this problem space.

The cascaded adapter design (S-Adapter for simple referring expressions, C-Adapter building on it for complex/implicit reasoning) with a frozen SAM3 backbone is a parameter-efficient approach that plausibly avoids catastrophic forgetting of concept-level grounding, and this claim is at least partially supported by the reported preservation of SAM3's concept-level scores.

The instruct-mask distribution alignment loss (KL divergence) and uncertainty-aware hard-region supervision are reasonable, well-motivated auxiliary objectives, and the ablation study convincingly shows each component (curriculum stages, alignment loss, hard-region loss) contributes positively to performance.

The three-stage semi-automatic data construction pipeline (MLLM annotation, agentic quality inspection with 100%-accuracy acceptance criterion, human-in-the-loop correction for long-tail failures) is a thoughtful and scalable strategy for producing instruction-mask pairs from existing segmentation datasets.
The paper commits to open-sourcing code, model weights, and fine-tuning workflows, and reports parameter counts/inference-mode differences, supporting reproducibility and practical adoption.
weaknesses: The paper explicitly states results are 'preliminary' and that 'comprehensive evaluation is ongoing,' which is a direct admission that the work is not yet complete; this undermines confidence in the central empirical claims and is atypical for a submission expected to stand on its own evidence.

All quantitative evaluation is conducted solely on a single benchmark (PACO-LVIS-Instruct) that the authors themselves constructed using the same MLLM-based pipeline used for training data; there is no evaluation on established, independent referring/reasoning segmentation benchmarks (e.g., RefCOCO/+/g, gRefCOCO, ReasonSeg) despite these being the standard comparison points for instruction-following segmentation and being mentioned as future work in the Discussion. This raises concerns about circularity and limits generalizability claims.

The comparison between SAM3-I and the SAM3+Agent baselines is confounded: SAM3-I is directly fine-tuned on the same distribution as the test set (PACO-LVIS-Instruct train split), while the agent baselines are used zero-shot with no adaptation to this benchmark or data distribution. This makes the reported gains (e.g., +12.4 gIoU) not a fair or convincing demonstration of architectural superiority versus simply the effect of in-domain fine-tuning.

No comparison against any prior reasoning-segmentation or referring-segmentation methods from the broader literature (e.g., LISA, which is even cited), making it hard to contextualize whether SAM3-I's absolute performance is competitive or merely internally consistent.

Key details on data quality and scale are missing: the proportion of instructions requiring human correction, agreement/quality metrics for the annotation-inspection loop, and potential biases introduced by using the same MLLM family (Qwen3-VL) for both data generation and the agent baseline are not reported, making it difficult to assess dataset reliability or fairness of comparisons.

The paper only evaluates on object/part-level instances from a single dataset domain (PACO-LVIS) with an N-to-1 instruction-instance structure, and the authors themselves acknowledge (in Discussion) that multi-instance/group reasoning and broader domain generalization are unaddressed, limiting the claimed scope of 'unifying concept and instruction-level reasoning within the SAM family.'

No error bars, statistical significance testing, or analysis of variance across runs/splits is provided given the relatively small effect sizes in some ablations (e.g., distribution alignment loss contributing ~1.6 gIoU).

strengths: Addresses a clear and practical limitation of SAM3 (its restriction to short NP prompts and heavy reliance on an external MLLM agent pipeline) with a well-motivated, parameter-efficient solution (frozen backbone + cascaded S-/C-Adapters).

The proposed alignment losses (instruction contrastive, parent-rank concept anchoring, mask distribution alignment, uncertainty-aware hard-region supervision) are individually well-justified and their contributions are validated through a thorough ablation study (Table 5), including single- vs. multi-stage training and single- vs. cascaded-adapter comparisons.

HMPL-Instruct is a carefully constructed dataset with a documented four-stage human-in-the-loop pipeline (automatic annotation, agentic inspection, human correction, dedicated tool for one-to-many subset annotation), and the paper provides good transparency via appendix diagrams, dataset statistics, and qualitative examples.

Empirical results are consistent and favorable across multiple settings: comparison with SAM3/SAM3 Agent, evaluation across instruction complexity levels (concept/simple/complex) and target cardinalities (one-to-one/one-to-many/one-to-all), object vs. part granularity, and generalization to external benchmarks (RefCOCO, Ref-ZOM) against strong baselines (LISA, UniPixel, ReLA).
Reasonable hyperparameter sensitivity analysis (ρ, m) and detailed implementation/reproducibility information (adapter dimensions, compute budget, training curriculum) are provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: The work is built directly on SAM3 (Carion et al., 2025), an extremely recent (essentially concurrent) and reportedly proprietary-leaning foundation model; this dependency raises concerns about external reproducibility and verifiability by readers who cannot access or fully evaluate the SAM3 backbone independently of this paper's claims.

The technical contribution is somewhat incremental — a bottleneck adapter + auxiliary alignment losses inserted into an existing frozen backbone — rather than a fundamentally new modeling idea; the core novelty largely rests on the specific combination of losses and the curated dataset rather than a new architectural or theoretical insight.

Dataset quality claims rely on an automatic MLLM annotation/inspection loop (same/similar underlying MLLM family, Qwen3-VL, used both for generation and inspection and possibly as a baseline agent), which could introduce self-consistency bias; no quantitative statistics are reported on inter-annotator agreement, rejection/correction rates, or human-verified accuracy of the final dataset beyond qualitative description.

Baseline comparisons, while reasonable given the novelty of the setting, are limited in number (LISA, UniPixel, ReLA, and a single SAM3-Agent configuration using one MLLM, Qwen3-VL-8B); it is unclear how sensitive the SAM3-Agent baseline's performance is to the choice or scale of the external MLLM, which affects the strength of the 'preserves efficiency while beating agent pipelines' claim.

The paper's own Limitations section acknowledges the one-to-many setting remains comparatively underexplored and data-imbalanced, and the framework does not extend to deeper semantic/conversational reasoning, which somewhat tempers the scope of the claimed contribution.

strengths: Addresses a clear, well-motivated gap: SAM3's agent-based pipeline for handling complex natural-language instructions is coarse (collapses to short NPs) and computationally expensive; SAM3-I removes the external MLLM loop and directly grounds instructions.

Technically well-designed instruction-aware cascaded adapter (S-Adapter/C-Adapter) with four complementary alignment losses (instruction contrastive, parent-rank concept anchoring, mask distribution KL, uncertainty-aware hard-region supervision), each ablated individually with sensible, interpretable results in Table 5.

Parameter-efficient design keeps the SAM3 backbone frozen (~0.3B added parameters) and empirically preserves original concept-level (PCS) performance, avoiding catastrophic forgetting while adding new capability.

New HMPL-Instruct dataset fills a real gap in the benchmark landscape by unifying concept/simple/complex instruction levels, object/part granularity, and one-to-one/one-to-many/one-to-all target cardinalities in a single resource (Table 1 comparison is informative).

Human-in-the-loop data construction pipeline (automatic annotation, agentic inspection, human correction, dedicated dual-panel tool for one-to-many subset selection) is described with good reproducibility detail, including annotator/inspector protocol.

Strong empirical results: outperforms SAM3 Agent (Qwen3-VL-8B) and other reasoning-segmentation baselines (LISA, UniPixel, ReLA) on HMPL-Instruct, RefCOCO, and Ref-ZOM while using a single-pass, smaller-parameter pipeline; ablations on multi-stage curriculum and cascaded vs. single adapter support key design choices.
Reasonable implementation/reproducibility details (hyperparameters, training compute, adapter architecture) and code/dataset release promised.
weaknesses: The training data (HMPL-Instruct) and the primary agent baseline (SAM3 Agent) both rely on the same MLLM family (Qwen3-VL), which raises a potential fairness/circularity concern: SAM3-I is effectively distilled from Qwen3-VL-generated/verified instructions, so part of its advantage over the Qwen3-VL-based agent baseline may reflect this asymmetry rather than purely architectural gains; the paper does not test agent baselines with a different/larger MLLM to control for this.

One-to-many instruction-instance data is obtained through a separate, purely human-driven annotation stage (Stage 4) that is acknowledged as limited in scale/diversity; the paper's own Limitations section flags this data imbalance, which constrains claims about the model's general subset-level/group reasoning ability.

Baseline comparisons, while reasonable (LISA, UniPixel, ReLA, SAM3 Agent), are not exhaustive relative to the fast-moving reasoning-segmentation literature, and no results are shown for stronger/larger agent MLLMs, alternative segmentation backbones, or robustness to paraphrased/adversarial instructions.

No variance/error bars or multiple-run statistics are reported for the main quantitative results, and dataset quality is validated mainly via MLLM-based 100%-consistency filtering plus limited human correction rather than an independent human quality/agreement study.

The dataset is derived from a single source (PACO-LVIS), limiting domain diversity; scaling to more diverse imagery is left as future work, so generalization beyond this benchmark's visual/instruction distribution is untested.

Method and dataset novelty, while solid engineering contributions, are largely combinatorial (known techniques: bottleneck adapters, contrastive/margin losses, KL alignment, curriculum training) applied to a new setting; the core insight is incremental relative to SAM3 and existing reasoning-segmentation work rather than a fundamentally new modeling idea.
